bounded_search.limitations: This is a declared high-relevance search, not proof that no other study exists. Closed full text, terminology drift, and unindexed older literature may hide additional material work.
queries: Inference of attitudes from nonverbal communication in two channels replication
Message Impact What Percentage is Nonverbal Hegstrom
bounded_search.result: One direct all-channel rebuttal, two related context-dependent empirical programs, and two methodological/propagation critiques were retained. No exact replication of the P1-plus-P2 derivation or validation of a universal fixed rule was identified.

claims.proposition: The circulated claim that 93 percent of communication is nonverbal is not a result established by the two 1967 experiments.
P1 found tone dominance when listeners inferred attitude from inconsistent isolated-word content and intonation without additional relationship information.
P2 found a stronger facial than vocal contribution in a two-channel task using the neutral word maybe and facial photographs.
The .07/.38/.55 values were proposed in P2's discussion as a cross-study weighted-sum extrapolation; neither 1967 experiment tested all three channels together.
The exact derivation of the .07 verbal coefficient is not disclosed in the two inspected 1967 papers or the inspected 1971 book pages.
The 1971 book repeats the equation, calls the numbers approximate, and limits use to one feeling dimension at a time.
The 1981 second edition is bibliographically identified, but its formula pages were not textually collated against 1971.
Hegstrom's direct all-channel reconsideration reported message-specific equations unlike both the fixed formula and one another.
Related Argyle experiments found nonverbal dominance but materially different ratios when cue strengths and attitude dimensions changed.
The broad rule propagated through public institutional material and a bounded web sample, but propagation supplies zero evidence that the scientific proposition is true.
The bounded search found one direct all-channel rebuttal and related follow-ups, but no exact replication of the two-study derivation or validation of a universal fixed rule.

lineage_edges.effect_on_independence: Count two participant-data roots because the papers report separate samples, while withholding any stronger person-level independence claim because participant identities are unavailable.
The named speakers do not overlap, but P2 leaves one author-speaker unnamed; speaker independence is therefore not fully closed.
Albert Mehrabian is common to both papers and P1 acknowledges Susan Ferris; the papers are not independent author programs.
Both report University of California Grant 2189; their Public Health Service grant identifiers differ. This is shared-program evidence, not shared-participant proof.
P2 reuses the neutral word maybe, which was one of P1's selected words; the material lineage is partially shared.
Both use prepared female-voice attitude recordings; P2 adds facial photographs and does not establish reuse of P1's recordings.
Both infer attitude from experimentally crossed channel cues; P1 crosses words and tone, while P2 crosses face and tone.
Both operationalize attitude as liking versus disliking, while their displayed scale procedures are not treated as identical instruments.
P2 is a declared continuation that cites P1 and later integrates its result; it is not an independent replication of the three-number rule.
The editions are one authorial work lineage and supply no new participant evidence; formula continuity into 1981 remains unresolved.
The .07/.38/.55 statement combines linked studies in P2's discussion. It is not a third participant-data root, and the exact .07 derivation remains no-credit.

lineages.independence: Distinct papers and participant groups inside one linked UCLA research program; P2 cites and integrates P1. Participant and speaker overlap across papers is not reported.
Author interpretation and book-edition lineage; no new participant evidence.
Separate author and all-channel research program; exact full-text participant and material details remain inaccessible.
Two related Oxford studies with shared author/program and different attitude dimensions; related evidence, not exact replication.
Same-author critique program; the 2007 website sample measures circulation, not scientific effect.
Separate institutional publications, each assigned zero empirical evidence credit.

propagation_ledger.limitation: Purposive convenience sample using one search engine; not a prevalence estimate.

content.question: What did the 7-38-55 weighting represent in the examined primary editions, how was it derived, and what supports or undercuts its circulation as a general rule of communication?

recommendation.author: GO
prohibited_interpretations: 93 percent of all communication is nonverbal
the two 1967 papers jointly tested three channels in one experiment
the coefficients are universally stable across messages, populations, cultures, or tasks
the missing .07 derivation has been recovered
recirculation counts are independent scientific support
recommendation.rationale: Proceed to a later Case 004 dossier if independent review closes the exact spans and calculations. The defensible case is that a narrow cross-study weighting was genuinely proposed, then generalized far beyond its scope, while a direct all-channel rebuttal found message-specific equations and the .07 derivation remains unresolved.
